case_info.scenario: A right-handed man in his 50s with a history of hepatitis C presented to clinic with a 1-year history of an enlarging painless nodule on his right index finger, which was now causing destruction of his nail. No preceding trauma was reported. On examination, an erythematous 15 × 10-mm well-circumscribed lobulated firm nodule was seen extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate of the right index finger, causing destruction of the adjacent nail plate (Figure 1A). The lesion did not transilluminate. No other findings were noted on full skin examination. A radiograph of the right hand revealed erosion of the distal phalanx, and 4-mm punch biopsies were taken from the proximal and distal pole of the nodule, highlighting similar histological features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, well-circumscribed, lobulated firm nodule extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate on the right index finger. Local invasion from the tumor has caused resultant lifting of the overlying nail plate, which appears thinned, split and shortened, failing to cover the distal nail bed. B, Punch biopsy showing acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion.
case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

dialogue_history.text: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) is a reasonable consideration given the painless nodule and bone erosion. However, TGCT typically arises from tendon sheaths or joints, especially in the fingers, and the description here—a well-circumscribed lobulated firm nodule extending from the dorsal DIPJ to the nail plate—also strongly suggests a glomus tumor, which classically presents with nail destruction and underlying bone erosion. Given the biopsies have been taken, the definitive next step is to review the histology for characteristic features (e.g., sheets of glomus cells, vascular channels) to confirm the diagnosis before planning surgical excision.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. 1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

2. Performance

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

case_info.scenario: A right-handed man in his 50s with a history of hepatitis C presented to clinic with a 1-year history of an enlarging painless nodule on his right index finger, which was now causing destruction of his nail. No preceding trauma was reported. On examination, an erythematous 15 × 10-mm well-circumscribed lobulated firm nodule was seen extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate of the right index finger, causing destruction of the adjacent nail plate (Figure 1A). The lesion did not transilluminate. No other findings were noted on full skin examination. A radiograph of the right hand revealed erosion of the distal phalanx, and 4-mm punch biopsies were taken from the proximal and distal pole of the nodule, highlighting similar histological features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, well-circumscribed, lobulated firm nodule extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate on the right index finger. Local invasion from the tumor has caused resultant lifting of the overlying nail plate, which appears thinned, split and shortened, failing to cover the distal nail bed. B, Punch biopsy showing acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion.
case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

Local invasion from the tumor has caused resultant lifting of the overlying nail plate, which appears thinned, split and shortened, failing to cover the distal nail bed. case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10
